tagline.text: A wide curtain of water in the Baganga forest, billed as the widest waterfall in the Davao Region

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: One day (an overnight stay is recommended from Davao City)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–2,500 (round-trip transport from Davao City included, per person)

children.text: Campawan Curtain Falls drops a broad sheet of water in the forest of Barangay Campawan in Baganga, and is described as the widest waterfall in the Davao Region. The trip is long and rough, but there is no entrance fee and you can walk right up to the water.

Campawan Curtain Falls is in Barangay Campawan, in the municipality of Baganga, Davao Oriental. The name "curtain" comes from the way the water does not fall in a single stream but spreads thin and wide along the whole rock ledge, like a drape. Local tourism listings and regional media describe it as the widest waterfall in the Davao Region, and some compare its shape to Tinuy-an Falls in Surigao del Sur. Heights are reported differently by different outlets; one Inquirer report describes a cataract about
high.

For a long time the falls were a hidden place visited only by nearby residents. Tourism began around 2015, when the road to Campawan was cleared and widened, and photos shared on social media spread the word. Even now there is almost no concrete development around the falls, only a few small stores and cottages, so the place keeps an unspoiled feel. There is no entrance fee, but parking is on private land and some owners charge a small amount.
That said, this is not an easy place to reach. Baganga is about
290 km

from Davao City along the coastal road, and Campawan is an upland village further inside. The last stretch is unpaved and bumpy. Many travelers therefore pair it with Aliwagwag Falls in nearby Cateel as a two-day, one-night waterfall trip. If time is tight, do not rush; allow generous time because the road is long.
According to map data, Barangay Campawan had about 2,100 residents in the 2020 census and lies at roughly

above sea level. Baganga's tourism listing says the barangay has many waterfalls, with Curtain Falls as the main attraction. Because Baganga combines coast and forest, you can also add beaches, a hot spring and a lake to a trip, but everything is far apart, so do not try to cover too much in one day. Enjoying a single waterfall properly and slowly taking in the forest and village scenery suits this place well. First-time visitors are advised to take a local driver or villager as a guide. The people who collect parking fees at the village entrance are usually residents who know the trail and the depth of the water best. Showing small thanks for small help is good manners on a village trip like this.

blocks.title: The widest curtain of water in the Davao Region

children.text: The biggest sight here is the water spreading wide along the whole rock ledge as it falls. Regional media describe it as the widest waterfall in the Davao Region.
You can easily walk up to the shallow pool below the falls. In the calm, shallow parts you can swim and play in the water, and some visitors enjoy a natural shower under the falling stream.

blocks.title: A forest walk across a river

children.text: From the parking area to the falls it is about
5–10 minutes
on foot, crossing a small river. The walk is short enough for children and older visitors to take slowly, but parts get wet, so sandals are best.
There is almost no concrete development and the surroundings are forest. On a weekday there are few people, so you can spend a quiet time with only the sound of the falls.

blocks.title: Cottages and shelter by the falls

children.text: There are small stores and cottages near the falls. Cottages are reported to rent from as little as about
, and even if you do not rent one you can leave your belongings in a shaded spot.

blocks.title: A good side angle for photos

children.text: Shooting from one side edge of the falls gives a photo that captures the full width of the water curtain. Going on a clear morning also brings out the color of the forest.
According to Baganga's tourism listing, Barangay Campawan has several waterfalls besides Curtain Falls. Local guides may point you to others, but the roads are rough, so check conditions beforehand.

Baganga lists attractions such as the white-sand beach and Sunrise Boulevard in Dapnan, and the hot spring and island in Kinablangan. Fitting one in before or after the falls enriches the trip. Check local conditions in advance.
Take a bus or van from a Davao City terminal toward Baganga or Cateel. Check the schedule at the terminal in advance.
Arrive in Baganga or Cateel, have lunch, and arrange a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) or tricycle. If you have luggage, a tricycle is more comfortable.
Head in along the unpaved road toward Campawan. The road is rough and slow, so plan to be back before dark.
Get off at the parking area, cross the river and walk to the falls. Swim and take photos.
Head back before sunset and spend the night in Baganga or Cateel.

The route to the falls passes through private land and village roads, so the whole schedule depends on the road. After heavy rain the river may be hard to cross, so check local conditions first. Do not try to see both the falls and the coast in one day; focusing on the falls alone is safer.

items.title: Combined with Aliwagwag Falls in Cateel
items.subtitle: Two waterfalls in two days

children.text: Arrive in Cateel and see Aliwagwag Falls first. Opening hours are reported differently by different sources, so check local notices.
After lunch, find a tricycle and head to Campawan Curtain Falls. One blog says it is about
2 hours
one way from Aliwagwag.
Swim at the falls, return by the same road and spend the night in Cateel or Baganga.
There are several nonstop flights from Manila (Ninoy Aquino International Airport) to Davao International Airport (DVO), and the flight takes about
2 hours
From Davao Airport, go into the city and on to a Davao City terminal.

items.title: From Davao City to Baganga or Cateel

children.text: Buses and vans run daily from Davao City terminals to Baganga or Cateel. Travel time varies by source, roughly
3–7 hours
One blog reports a van fare from the Ecoland terminal to Cateel of about
and about
3 hours
. Schedules and fares change, so confirm locally.
Baganga is about
290 km
from Davao City via Mati City.

items.title: The last leg by habal-habal or tricycle

children.text: From Baganga or Cateel to Campawan, hire a habal-habal or tricycle for the day.
A one-day habal-habal hire has been reported at about
, and one review gives about
for a round-trip tricycle from Aliwagwag. Both are information from several years ago, so negotiate and confirm current prices.
The road is unpaved and slippery when it rains.

Davao Oriental is on the east coast and tends to get heavy rain in the cooler months. The best time for plentiful water and the time when the road is in good shape may differ. Considering the unpaved road and the river crossing, the relatively drier months are safer.
The falls look more impressive when rain increases the flow, but on the same day the river may swell and become hard to cross. Check local conditions before you leave.

The exact wet and dry seasons vary from year to year, so put the forecast just before departure and local conditions first. It helps to remember that rain is more frequent in this east-coast region during the northeast monsoon.

rows: The road can turn to mud and the river can rise.

There is almost no lodging around Campawan. Most people stay in Baganga town or Cateel and visit in a day. Baganga and Cateel have small guesthouses and inns, but not many, so look in advance for peak season and weekends.

There are small stores near the falls where you can buy drinks and light snacks, but do not expect meals. Bring a packed lunch and plenty of water before leaving town. This is also a place where you need to carry enough cash.

Baganga town has a market and eateries where you can easily find local meals such as grilled fish, chicken and rice. Eat in town or in Cateel and buy snacks and water before heading up to the falls. There are also lodgings and restaurants near Aliwagwag Falls, and many people who combine the two waterfalls stay on the Cateel side. Room rates and booking methods change, so check online maps and reviews for the latest.
Arranging a tricycle or habal-habal driver in advance is easier; agree first on the round-trip time and waiting charge.
Parts of the route get wet, so wear sandals or water shoes and bring a change of clothes and a waterproof bag.
Phone signal may be weak, so download an offline map.
Take your trash back with you. It is a place cared for by villagers, so protecting the environment matters.
Combining it with Aliwagwag Falls in a two-day trip makes the long travel more worthwhile.
Bring plenty of small cash (₱20 and ₱50 bills).
Before leaving, phone Baganga tourism staff or your driver to check the road condition to the falls.
Weather in Southeast Asia changes suddenly, so bring a light raincoat.
When taking photos of the falls, shoot from the shallow edge, and keep your camera and phone in a waterproof pouch for peace of mind.
Most payments are in cash, so finish exchanging and withdrawing money in Davao City before you leave.
The last stretch of road to Campawan is unpaved, and the river can swell and become dangerous when it rains. Do not cross the river on days of heavy rain.
The fees and road conditions mentioned come from articles and reviews several years old, so check the latest with Baganga's municipal office or a local driver before going.
Avoid traveling the unpaved mountain road after dark.
Rocks below the falls are mossy and slippery, and the water may suddenly get deep in places.
After rain the water volume and current change. Follow what locals tell you.
Security and travel restrictions in eastern Davao Oriental can change over time, so check travel advisories.
